claims.text: Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 forms several primary non-eutectic crystalline phases during solidification.
Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 exhibits a complex, multistep crystallization sequence under conventional thermal treatment.
The proposed intervention is a short-duration, high-rate pulse reheating step applied immediately after slower cooling.
Pulse reheating after slow cooling will kinetically bypass extensive primary crystallization.
Pulse reheating will increase amorphous retention in Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20.
Pulse reheating will increase the thermal stability of Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20.
The pulse temperature should be above the glass transition and below the crystallization onset measured by DSC.
Limiting the hold to a few seconds will minimize atomic diffusion.
Reducing time in the temperature range critical for primary crystallization suppresses crystal nucleation and growth.
Suppression of nucleation and growth preserves an amorphous-like structure or a higher amorphous-phase volume fraction.
Rapid pulse reheating creates a thermal gradient that quickly relaxes the alloy structure.
The short pulse provides insufficient time for atoms to rearrange into crystalline nuclei.
Pulse-treated samples will have a higher amorphous-phase fraction than samples subjected to conventional gradual reheating.
Pulse-treated samples will exhibit a higher crystallization-onset temperature during subsequent reheating than conventionally reheated samples.
Rapid cooling followed by slow or gradual reheating produces extensive primary crystalline phases, multistep crystallization, and lower thermal stability in this alloy.
Outside the proposed temperature and duration window, either insufficient structural relaxation or unwanted crystallization may occur.
The peak temperature, ramp rate, and hold time require optimization because reheating kinetics and nucleation barriers are not established for this alloy.

contradictions.description: Primary crystallization is said to occur during solidification, but the intervention is applied only after slow cooling. A post-solidification reheating pulse cannot temporally bypass primary crystallization that has already occurred, and no remelting or amorphization step is specified.

The stated comparison is standard rapid cooling followed by gradual reheating, whereas the experiment prepares both groups using identical slow cooling and varies only reheating. Thus the experimental control does not match the stated baseline.

The mechanism describes relaxation and prevention of additional crystallization below the crystallization onset, but the outcome requires an increased amorphous fraction after prior slow-cooling crystallization. No mechanism is given for converting already formed crystalline phases back into amorphous material.
